metadata.title: Obama Endorses Angie Nixon for Florida Senate Seat

sources.news_title: Obama backs Angie Nixon as Trump, DeSantis endorse Ashley Moody
sources.text:
Obama backs Angie Nixon as Pres. Trump, Gov. DeSantis endorse Ashley Moody
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (CBS12) — Former President Barack Obama is throwing his support behind Florida Democrat Angie Nixon in the U.S. Senate race, urging voters to back the state lawmaker as Election Day approaches.
Obama praised Nixon's work as an organizer and state lawmaker, citing her support for a $15 minimum wage, efforts to protect access to books, and opposition to Republican-led congressional redistricting.
"That's why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. Senator," Obama said in the video. "So cast your vote for Angie Nixon on or before November 3."
Nixon is challenging Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, who was appointed to the Senate by Gov. Ron DeSantis in January 2025 after Marco Rubio left the seat to become U.S. Secretary of State.
Moody has received endorsements from President Donald Trump, Governor Ron DeSantis, U.S. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama and U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for Florida governor.
See also: Pres. Trump expected to vote in person in Palm Beach after casting mail ballot in March
Obama said he and Nixon both began their careers as organizers, adding that her work has focused on standing up for working families and their rights:
When working families were struggling to get by, Angie fought for a $15 minimum wage. When politicians in the state capitol tried to tell people what they could and couldn't read, she opened a bookstore to let you decide."
Nixon said the endorsement comes as her campaign focuses on affordability, health care and protecting Floridians' rights.
"Having President Obama's support means so much to me," Nixon said. "This campaign has always been about building a grassroots movement to fight for everyday Floridians who are being priced out and left behind."
She said the endorsement would provide additional momentum as the campaign enters its final days.
Obama's endorsement comes as early voting is underway across Florida. Nixon's campaign said voters can watch the endorsement video on her social media channels and find early voting locations through her campaign website.

sources.news_title: Obama endorses Nixon, Jolly in last-minute campaign boost
Obama endorses Nixon after cry for support to party leadership
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama endorsed Angie Nixon’s (D-FL) bid to unseat Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) on Saturday, marking his support for the progressive insurgent’s uphill battle in the red state.
Obama’s formal backing comes after Nixon, who is black, alleged earlier this week that assumptions about Florida being perceived as racist had held back Democratic support for her campaign.
Recommended Stories
In a short video message released days before voters head to the polls, Obama hailed Nixon’s fight against redistricting efforts favoring the GOP, and her support for a $15 minimum wage, saying, “Angie has spent her career standing up for you.”
“Real change starts when regular folks stand up for what’s right,” Obama said. “She was on the front lines, trying to stop it. Different issues, different moments. One leader, willing to stand up again and again for what’s right. That’s why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. senator.”
Obama’s endorsement comes as he was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win Florida, formerly considered a purple state. Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, said she was “honored” by the endorsement in a post to X.
Her win against Alex Vindman, a nationally recognized Democrat with a significant fundraising advantage, in Florida’s August primary garnered significant attention, as it signaled the rising power of progressives in the state.
Obama’s involvement in the Florida race comes after he endorsed David Jolly (D-FL) in the state’s gubernatorial election. Jolly, a more centrist Democrat, is mounting a spirited challenge to his Republican opponent Byron Donalds to succeed Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL).
Florida isn’t the only state Obama has dabbled with in the midterm elections. On Saturday, he set out to hold a series of events backing Democrats in Ohio and Michigan.

In Ohio, lines on Saturday morning wrapped for blocks around the Cleveland Public Auditorium for Obama’s rally with Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton.
Later in the day, Obama is headed to Detroit to campaign with Democrat Senate nominee Abdul el Sayed, who is embroiled in a tight campaign against GOP candidate Mike Rogers.

sources.news_title: First Clinton, and now Jolly picks up an endorsement from Obama
Barack Obama endorses Angie Nixon for Senate
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama continues to weigh in on Florida statewide races, endorsing state Rep. Angie Nixon for Senate less than 24 hours after announcing his support for gubernatorial candidate David Jolly.
In a video running a little more than a minute, Obama mentioned that Nixon, like her, started off as a community organizer.
He cited her fight for a $15 minimum wage and her stances against book censorship in schools and Congressional redistricting in the Florida House.
“She was on the front lines, trying to stop it. Different issues, different moments. One leader, willing to stand up again and again for what’s right. That’s why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. Senator,” Obama said.
The endorsement continues a recent trend of national Democratic leaders, such as U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, showing support for Nixon, who wasn’t the preference of most establishment Democrats ahead of the August Primary.
Nixon said she’s “honored to share that President Obama is supporting our campaign for the U.S. Senate.”
“Obama and I both started as organizers in our communities, because we immediately understood that real changes come from regular folks joining the fight,” she added.
Moody’s campaign dismissed the endorsement.
“No surprise the spiritual founder of the DSA endorses current Florida mouthpiece for the DSA. Obama is about to go 0-3 on Florida Senate endorsements over the last three election cycles,” said the Moody War Room.

sources.news_title: Obama endorses progressive insurgent Angie Nixon for Senate in Florida
Obama Endorses Angie Nixon for Florida Senate Seat
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama threw his support behind Jacksonville Democrat Angie Nixon on Saturday, releasing a one-minute video urging Florida voters to back her bid for U.S. Senate. The endorsement lands with just over a week left before the November 3 general election, as new polling shows the race tightening between Nixon and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody.
In the video, Obama praised Nixon's record of public service, saying, “And Angie has spent her career standing up for you,” according to Politico. He went further in his endorsement of the state representative, declaring, “That's why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. Senator,” per Florida Politics. Nixon, who has represented a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House since 2020, is running as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Florida's 2026 general election, as reported by First Coast News.
A Jacksonville Organizer's Path to the Ballot
Nixon describes herself as a fifth-generation Jacksonville native, according to the Lakewood Ranch Beacon. Before entering politics, she worked as a union and community organizer, and she helped push for a Florida referendum that raised the state's minimum wage to $15 an hour, the same Politico report notes. She also owns Cafe Resistance, a Jacksonville bookstore and cafe that stocks titles some Florida schools have sought to remove from their libraries, per the outlet's reporting.
Nixon's campaign platform centers on working families, health care access and political accountability, according to Essence. She won her party's primary with 56.1 percent of the vote, defeating Alex Vindman, who took 43.9 percent, the same outlet reports. The financial gap between the two primary rivals was stark: Vindman had reported raising $16.7 million by mid-year, while Nixon had reported a little over $625,000, according to Essence's reporting. Her campaign says her average donation runs under $30.
Polling Shows a Narrowing Race
A University of North Florida poll taken October 12 through 19 found Moody leading Nixon 49% to 45%, with 5% undecided, the same poll noted. That margin has tightened since July, when Moody's lead stood at eight points, 50% to 42%, per the Florida Politics report, which cited a sample of 1,471 likely Florida midterm voters and a margin of error of plus or minus 2.81 percentage points. Nixon performed especially well among third-party and no-party voters, leading that group 50% to 35%, according to the same polling data.
Turnout modeling in the poll projected an electorate made up of 45% Republicans, 33% Democrats and 22% third-party and no-party voters. Florida Division of Elections figures cited in the report showed Democrats ahead by 54,371 returned mail ballots, though Republican ballots were completing the round trip more reliably, 41.3% to 38.8%. Republicans also held a narrow early-voting edge, 69,280 to 68,650, as of the same update.
National Democrats Rally Behind Nixon's Bid
Obama's video adds a high-profile name to a list of national Democrats who have stepped in for Nixon, including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, according to Florida Politics' earlier coverage. Her listed endorsements also include U.S. Sens. Chris Murphy and Elizabeth Warren, along with several members of the U.S. House, per the Lakewood Ranch Beacon. Florida has grown more Republican since Donald Trump's political rise, and Obama remains the last Democratic presidential candidate to carry the state, Politico notes.
Moody, the Republican incumbent, has a presidential endorsement from Trump, according to First Coast News. Nixon faces Moody in the November 3 general election; reporting on the ballot's full field has varied, with some accounts naming a no-party-preference candidate in the race and others describing it as a head-to-head contest between Nixon and Moody. First Coast News reports that Nixon has said Obama's support means a great deal to her, and that her campaign is focused on building a grassroots movement for everyday Floridians facing rising costs. Her campaign has also said it aims to make health care more affordable and to protect families' rights, the outlet reports, while Nixon has opposed Republican efforts to redraw congressional maps in ways she says would deny voters a voice.
